questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a colloid from a true solution
questions.stem: Reading the data table, a sample shows particles 1 to 1000 nm that do not settle on standing; classify it.

options.text: It is a colloid since particles are dispersed but not dissolved.
It is a colloid because the particles scatter a light beam.
options.misconception: assumes Tyndall scattering alone defines every colloid

options.text: It is a true solution because all dissolved species are ions.
options.misconception: confuses dispersed particles with dissolved ions

options.text: It is a suspension because the particles exceed molecular size.
options.misconception: treats any large dispersed particle as a suspension

questions.explanation: Colloidal particles are larger than molecules yet stay dispersed without settling, unlike true solutions where solute dissolves. The tempting distractor conflates scattering with definition.
questions.hint: Compare particle size and settling behavior.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the Tyndall effect evidences
questions.stem: A beam of light shone through a sample produces a visible cone; what does this evidence?

options.text: The sample contains ions that absorb visible light strongly.
The sample is a colloid with dispersed particles scattering light.
The sample is pure solvent with no solute present.
options.misconception: assumes pure solvent scatters a light beam

options.text: The sample is a suspension that will settle within minutes.
options.misconception: confuses a stable colloid with a settling suspension

questions.explanation: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by dispersed colloidal particles, distinguishing colloids from true solutions. It does not imply rapid settling.
